name: Amira Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, a mid-level carpenter on a crew putting up interior walls at the new library. I have a vocational trade certificate, and I measure bays, fix studs and cut board around pipes. I like seeing a room take shape; carrying sheets through a tight stairwell is the tiring part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives a local bus, we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and we have about three months of expenses saved. I earn typical site pay and there are some similar building jobs nearby. I use AI every day for timber order lists and quick drawing checks, but I measure the actual wall before ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the framing crew that AI can sort a timber order faster, and I already use it each morning. The wall still needs somebody to find a level line on a lumpy slab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small productivity gain suits me because my own paid site work continues. With three months of expenses saved and a mortgage, I like the extra time, but I don't want to pretend a calendar app pays our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting out the library's interior walls and use the AI order sheet I already make each day. Before sending it, I'll check board lengths against the measured bays, then put any hours saved into finishing the actual fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job and fairly pleased with the breathing room. I know where the software helps because I test it against the wall in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the order sheet need changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the order sheet proposed standard-length boards for a bay with a hidden pipe chase. I changed the cut list before anything went to the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the time saving change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might get home a little earlier on an ordering day, which helps with school pick-up when my partner drives the late bus. I would still work my usual site hours and put the mortgage wage first.

say: **Daily AI ordering** saves a little time on timber lists.
**Measured walls** still decide how boards are cut and fitted.
think: My **site wage** continues and the mild change gives me useful time.
Three months of **expenses saved** leave the mortgage visible, even in an easy picture.
do: **Keep** setting out library walls and checking board lengths against measured bays.
**Use** the existing daily AI order sheet for timber deliveries.
feel: **Calm** about continued carpentry work and small time savings.
S0.quote: The wall still needs somebody to find a level line on a lumpy slab.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI daily** for material orders, but checks bay dimensions and pipe chases before buying.
Her **three-month reserve** supports calm only while the familiar site wage continues alongside her partner's bus income.

steps.text: Keep setting out library walls and checking actual board lengths

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the builders' chat that AI will probably draw purchase lists and chase deliveries before a robot lifts a stud wall. I want the carpenters shown the new drawings early enough to spot mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may send more jobs through fewer people, which could mean longer site days for us. My hands-on work looks needed for now, but a bad schedule could eat into the school pick-up we share with my bus-driver partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask to try the updated planning tool on the library's next two rooms and learn how to change its quantities rather than just read them. I'll compare my measured timber use with its list, then show the foreman the gaps before it orders the next load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pace of site days, not expecting a lost wage next month. I can learn the new screen faster than a truck can deliver the wrong boards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change before an AI order goes out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the actual pipe chase on the drawing and correct the order before it reaches the timber yard. The foreman can then see the change instead of an unexplained shortage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two rooms make a useful test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next two rooms have different wall lengths and one has ducts. If the list catches both, I'll use the edit controls on a larger room; if it misses them, I want the manual check kept.

say: **AI planning** may speed buying while hands-on wall fitting remains.
Carpenters need **early drawings** to catch bad quantities before delivery.
think: My own **site wage** looks intact, but a rushed schedule could stretch the day.
School collection still needs a **predictable finish** for my partner and me.
do: **Learn** editing controls on updated site planner for two library rooms.
**Compare** measured timber use with AI quantities before next load.
feel: **Uneasy** about longer days, while the site wage remains secure.
S1.quote: I can learn the new screen faster than a truck can deliver the wrong boards.
fieldNote: She commits to **learning edit controls** on two real rooms, a new use beyond her existing daily AI ordering.
Her concern is **schedule pressure** on school collection; she does not predict a wage loss in this slower scenario.

steps.text: Learn updated site planner editing controls on two library rooms
Compare measured timber use with AI quantities before ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI by 2028 might price and plan our framing jobs, then capable site robots around 2031 could put the walls up. I'd want actual paid roles named before anyone sells this as a better building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 48 when robots can handle our physical work. If our contractor cuts the framing crew, three months of savings and some other local builders are a bridge, not a long wage replacement for a mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the foreman which robot supplier and crew plan the company is testing. I'll sign up for the first paid machine-setter training if the company offers an actual place with wages through the course; if it doesn't, I'll apply to advertised building maintenance jobs while I still have work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can act before the machines reach our site. I would rather make a measured move than wait for the crew board to come down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that a course only counts if it keeps my pay coming while I attend. Our three-month mortgage reserve can cover a gap, but I won't gamble it on a site robot training advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make machine-setter training real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a named trainer, paid training hours and practice on the supplier's actual machine. If the course is real, I'll attend even if someone else on site thinks the old method will last forever.

say: **2028 thinking AI** could price framing jobs before robots build walls around 2031.
Workers need **named paid roles** and training places as site machines arrive.
think: At about **48**, a smaller framing crew could threaten my mortgage wage.
Three months of **savings** and some local builders give choices, not years of income.
do: **Ask** foreman about supplier trials and future framing crew numbers this week.
**Attend** paid machine-setter training if a wage-backed place is offered.
**Apply** for advertised building maintenance jobs if no paid training appears.
feel: **Anxious** about possible crew cuts, with several concrete options.
S2.quote: Our three-month mortgage reserve can cover a gap, but I won't gamble it on a site robot training advert.
fieldNote: She moves quickly toward **machine-setter training**, but only if a real place covers wages and practice on the actual machine.
The fallback **job search** requires advertised maintenance posts and the absence of a paid training route; saved cash is not new saving.

steps.text: Ask foreman about robot supplier trials and framing crew plan
Attend machine-setter training if offered paid place with wages
Apply while employed for advertised maintenance jobs if no paid training appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site that 2031 thinking AI could take over estimates, while 2034 robots might do the hands-on framing. Five years is a fair chance to trial machines on a spare section and see who still needs to be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 51 when capable robots reach the building work. My family still needs wages, but I can work toward a site plant qualification before any framing crew cut, if the cost and hours fit our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll take a free evening introduction to site plant controls and practise the safety checks. If the contractor funds the recognised machine-operation certificate and keeps my pay during assessment days, I'll enrol next term; otherwise I'll keep the framing wage and look for a paid route elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful, but anxious about the wage if site machines shrink crews. Five years lets me build proof of a second skill without leaving a job first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe machine trial look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a machine on an empty mock wall with an instructor, not a live site full of other trades. We need to see whether it spots an uneven floor before it fixes the first stud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which numbers decide whether you take the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the course fee, paid release days and whether nearby builders accept the certificate. My three months of reserve are for our mortgage, so I won't pay a large fee on a guess.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes estimates before robots frame walls around 2034.
A **mock wall trial** would test an uneven floor without putting other trades nearby.
think: At about **51**, I still need the site wage if fewer framers are hired.
A **second qualification** is feasible if fees and assessment wages are covered.
do: **Attend** free evening introduction to site plant controls this month.
**Enrol** in recognised operation certificate if employer funds fees and paid assessment release.
**Keep** framing while looking for paid training if funding is refused.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with time to gain skills.
S3.quote: My three months of reserve are for our mortgage, so I won't pay a large fee on a guess.
fieldNote: She starts **actual introductory learning** now and sets explicit employer funding and wage conditions for the recognised certificate.
A five-year window lets her **test a mock wall** while protecting the framing wage and mortgage reserve.

steps.text: Attend free evening introduction to site plant controls this month
Enrol in recognised operation certificate if fees and paid release funded
Keep framing while seeking paid training if funding refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 may run the estimates and capable site robots around 2039 may frame walls. A decade gives us time to see which machines work around real stairs and pipes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 56 when robots do the physical site work, and both children will be older. We still need to pay the mortgage, but ten years is long enough to move into site coordination if the qualifications lead to actual jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the daily AI order sheets accurate and enrol in a part-time site coordination course next year if the fee fits our budget after mortgage payments. Each year I'll check actual local vacancies and ask the contractor for supervised planning shifts before I apply for a posted coordination role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about future site jobs, but interested in the longer route. I can still frame walls while learning to run a better handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a coordination vacancy worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see a real posting with a wage that covers the mortgage and hours that fit school or later family needs. I wouldn't trade a paid carpentry week for a job title on a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new site coordinator first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A coordinator has to pass on the actual measurements to the next trade, not just upload a tidy model. I would bring the electrician to the wall before closing it so they can find the cable chase.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes estimates before site robots frame walls around 2039.
A decade permits **site coordination training** tied to real vacancies.
think: At about **56**, I may still need the mortgage wage when robots reach sites.
Older children and a long runway improve my **room to plan**, without guaranteeing a new job.
do: **Keep** checking daily AI timber orders against measured site bays.
**Enrol** in part-time site coordination course if fees fit after mortgage payments.
**Apply** for posted coordination role if wage and hours fit household needs.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-run roles, interested in a gradual shift.
S4.quote: I wouldn't trade a paid carpentry week for a job title on a brochure.
fieldNote: Her longer plan is **conditional training**, followed by a posted coordination vacancy with wages and hours that suit the household.
She continues **measured site work** and sees coordination as a possible move, without assuming a place will exist.

steps.text: Keep checking daily AI timber orders against measured bays
Enrol in part-time site coordination course if fee fits mortgage budget
Apply for posted site coordinator role if wage and hours fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is hardest because capable site robots around 2031 could cut framing hours while the children and mortgage still need wages. A paid machine-setter place and a clear crew plan would let me move early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a robot's first wall after it leaves the test bay. A neat digital frame will not tell the electrician where the hidden pipe chase is. I want a real trade worker at that handover.

headlineQuote: A neat digital frame will not tell the electrician where the hidden pipe chase is.
portrait: **Amira**, 43, is a mid-level site carpenter with a vocational trade certificate and typical construction pay.
She and her bus-driver partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with three months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** for timber orders, but checks quantities against real bays, pipes and uneven floors.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about framing hours; she seeks paid machine training and tests new tools early.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring site robots around 2031 while mortgage payments and children's costs still rely on wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid machine-setter place** and a clear framing crew plan would help her move before hours are cut.
